info.bio:
Lionel Hampton (Louisville, 20 de abril de 1908 - Nueva York, 31 de agosto de 2002). Vibrafonista, pianista, batería, cantante y director estadounidense de jazz.

Hampton fue el primer vibrafonista del jazz y una de sus grandes figuras desde los años treinta. Su estilo es fundamentalmente el del jazz clásico, o mainstream jazz, con fuertes vínculos con el jazz de las big bands, esto es, con el swing.

Hampton comenzó como batería, tocando en su juventud con los Chicago Defender Newsboys' Band.

scenes.name: Benny Goodman, el rey del swing
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La Depresión hunde la venta de discos y el fin de la ley seca desmitifica el jazz, pero la radio en cadena crea el estrellato: managers como Hammond, Glaser o Mills median entre arte y masas. Goodman, hijo de inmigrantes judíos de Maxwell Street y clarinetista de técnica clásica, prepara su triunfo en el programa Let's Dance de la NBC (con arreglos de Fletcher Henderson, «King Porter Stomp», «Sometimes I'm Happy») y estalla en el Palomar Ballroom el 21 de agosto de 1935: nace la era del swing y el fenómeno de fans que anuncia a Sinatra, Elvis o los Beatles. Con Hammond rompe la barrera racial en sus combos (Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton, Charlie Christian), lleva el jazz al Carnegie Hall en 1938 y encarga obras a Bartók, Copland y Hindemith. Gene Krupa populariza al batería como estrella; Bunny Berigan, Harry James, Ziggy Elman, Jess Stacy y luego Mel Powell y Eddie Sauter dan a la banda una modernidad propia, la que el bebop no siguió. Las bandas blancas tuvieron ventajas que Henderson nunca tuvo.

scenes.name: Roy Eldridge y Lionel Hampton
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Dos enlaces de la era del swing. Roy Eldridge, para muchos colegas el mayor trompetista de su generación, nunca triunfa como líder; sus solos con su octeto y con Krupa («Let Me Off Uptown») rompen barreras raciales, y aunque toca en el Minton's y podría haberse pasado al bop, queda como el eslabón entre Armstrong y Gillespie. Lionel Hampton, que había sido batería y cantante imitador de Armstrong, descubre por casualidad un vibráfono en un estudio de la NBC y lo convierte en instrumento de jazz: torrentes de notas, ornamentación barroca y swing a raudales en el cuarteto de Goodman.

scenes.name: Bebop: Charlie Parker y Dizzy Gillespie
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: El jazz siempre fue moderno, pero el jazz moderno no nace de Ellington ni de Goodman en el Carnegie Hall, sino de jam sessions nocturnas de músicos de grupo (el guitarrista de Goodman, el bajista de Ellington, el saxo de Hines, el trompetista de Calloway): un movimiento underground que inaugura la mentalidad de búnker del jazz progresista. Nuevas melodías sobre los acordes de viejos standards, combos con saxo y trompeta al unísono, solos rapidísimos de corcheas regulares que empiezan y acaban en partes débiles, notas de tensión, sustituciones II-V, y una sección rítmica heredera de Kansas City con «bombas» de batería (Kenny Clarke, Max Roach). Charlie Parker, formado con Buster Smith y Jay McShann y en los discos de Lester Young, une el blues de Kansas City con Stravinsky y Hindemith; Dizzy Gillespie, heredero de Roy Eldridge y alumno de Mario Bauza, es el virtuoso y el showman. En 1945 graban para Guild y Savoy («Groovin' High», «Salt Peanuts», «Ko Ko»); Parker se hunde en California (la sesión de «Lover Man», Camarillo), vuelve con un estilo más relajado («Embraceable You», «Parker's Mood») y muere en 1955 con treinta y cuatro años y el cuerpo de un hombre de sesenta. Para los músicos negros, el bebop es también la exigencia de ser reconocidos como artistas.

podcast.title: Early Adoption of Precision Bass
podcast.body: Lionel Hampton's band is believed to be the first to incorporate the Fender Precision Bass into their lineup, with Monk Montgomery as their bassist. This marked a significant early adoption of the electric bass in a professional setting. "As far as we can tell, Lionel Hampton's band was the first to incorporate the P-Base. It appears that his guy was named Monk Montgomery."

podcast.title: Early Afterbeat Drumming Style
podcast.body: In his autobiography, Lionel Hampton described his drumming style before switching to the vibraphone, stating he was already playing with a "heavy afterbeat," which he identified as the "rock and roll beat" that wouldn't become popular until the 1950s. He aimed for people to dance, have a good time, and clap their hands to his drumming, but this style was never recorded. "I was already playing with a heavy afterbeat, getting that rock and roll beat that wouldn't even get popular until the 1950s."

podcast.title: Formed Own Big Band
podcast.body: A couple of years after the 1939 "Flying Home" recording, Lionel Hampton left Benny Goodman's band to form his own big band. This band became a pioneer in "Jump band music," which was rooted in swing but emphasized riffs and amplified instruments, eventually evolving into rhythm and blues. "A couple of years later, Lionel Hampton left Goodman's band to form his own big band and flying home became their signature song."

podcast.title: Influence on Early R&B
podcast.body: Lionel Hampton's band was one of the significant influences on early R&B, alongside Count Basie's, contributing to the blend of jump band and classy jazz that characterized the genre. "The Count Basie band was, like Lionel Hamptons, one of the bands that had most influenced early R&B..."

podcast.title: Influence on James Brown's Funk
podcast.body: Lionel Hampton's style of jazz and swing, along with Count Basie's, heavily influenced James Brown's much later funk recordings. Brown's music is seen as the logical progression of the style these musicians developed. "That style of music wouldn't show up in his earlier records, which were mostly fairly standard vocal group R&B, but if you listen to his much later funk recordings, they owe a lot to Basie and Lionel Hampton."

podcast.title: Most Respected Vibraphone Musician
podcast.body: To this day, Lionel Hampton is considered probably the most respected musician ever to play the vibes. His profound contributions significantly shaped the instrument's role and reputation in jazz. "Indeed, to this day, Hampton is probably the most respected musician ever to play the vibes."

podcast.title: Paved Way for Jackie Robinson
podcast.body: Lionel Hampton often claimed that Benny Goodman's decision to hire him and Teddy Wilson, and later other black musicians, directly "paved the way for Robinson's more well-known achievement" of breaking the color barrier in baseball, which occurred nine years later. "In fact, Lionel Hampton would often later claim that it was Goodman hiring him and Wilson and later other black musicians that paved the way for Robinson's more well-known achievement."

podcast.title: Quincy Jones Joins Brass Section
podcast.body: Around his 20th birthday, Quincy Jones scored a performing break by joining the brass section of vibraphonist and band leader Lionel Hampton, playing trumpet alongside Art Farmer and Clifford Brown in Hampton's orchestra. "Around his 20th birthday, Jones scored a break as a performer, joining the brass section of vibraphonist and band leader Lionel Hampton."

podcast.title: Rock Music Pioneer Recognition
podcast.body: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, as big bands lost popularity, Hampton became a great B-bop musician, but he was also recognized by rock musicians as a pioneer. He appeared in the 1957 Alan Fried film "Mr. Rock and Roll" as the only jazz musician alongside rock and roll stars like Little Richard and Clyde McFatter. "But he was also recognised by the rock musicians as a pioneer."

podcast.title: Trained as Drummer
podcast.body: Before becoming a vibraphone player, Hampton trained as a drummer and was often billed as "the fastest drummer in the world." His unique melodic sensibility allowed him to become the premier soloist on the new instrument, the vibraphone. "Hampton had trained us at rumour before becoming a vibraphone player and was often billed as the fastest drummer in the world."

podcast.title: Vibraphone Pioneer
podcast.body: Lionel Hampton was a virtuoso vibraphone player who "more or less defined how that instrument was incorporated into jazz," and appears to be the first person to use it on a recorded jazz track (Louis Armstrong's "Memories of You" in 1930). At the time, the vibraphone was so new its name wasn't settled, and Hampton played an instrument branded "Vibrahap," which he called it for life. "He was a virtuoso vibraphoneist who more or less defined how that instrument was incorporated into jazz."
